paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Bynum took place near Driver, in Nansemond County, Virginia, in the early morning of December 19, 1903, when a crowd threatened the life of Bynum, a Black man accused of burning the barn and stables of his landlord, John L. Bond. To keep him from the crowd, Justice Morris held a preliminary hearing at about 3 a.m. by the light of the fire, held Bynum for court, and had him taken to jail. The image of a night court lit by the burning barn carried the story into papers across the country.

Bynum, described as about thirty years old, lived in one of Bond's houses on his farm about ten miles from Suffolk. According to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, he refused to work or pay rent, and on December 18 Bond had him locked out. A Maryland weekly later called him "a discharged employee."

About 10 o'clock that night, while Bond was out fox-hunting, his barn and stables burned. Bynum was accused of setting the fire; the Times-Dispatch called the evidence "circumstantial, but strong," noting that he could not account for his whereabouts and was "said to have made threats." The Washington Evening Star's Suffolk correspondent went further and wrote that Bynum "fired" the buildings, while also calling him "an alleged firebug."

A "clamoring crowd" gathered and, in the Times-Dispatch's words, "threatened his life." Justice Morris convened what the Evening Star called a "hurry court" at about 3 a.m., by the light of the still-burning fire, and committed Bynum for trial. Morris and an officer named Branch said Bynum's life had been in danger and that only doubt about his guilt had let them save him. Branch then took him to jail by a roundabout route.

Bynum was reported under arrest and held for court, or "bound over for trial" in some versions of the wire. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowd is named.

The first reports were special dispatches from Suffolk to the Evening Star on December 19 and the Times-Dispatch on December 20, under the headlines "FIREBUG ESCAPED LYNCHING" and "DAYLIGHT COURT TO SAVE HIS NECK." Both treated the officers as rescuers, and the Evening Star presented Bynum's guilt as settled. The Alexandria Gazette's Virginia news column added that Bond was "a prominent resident" and that Bynum, "colored," had "narrowly escaped lynching."

A short Norfolk wire item ran on December 21 in the New-York Tribune, the Washington Times, the Savannah Morning News, the Indianapolis Journal, the Saint Paul Globe and papers in Nebraska and Connecticut. Its headlines played up the irony of a man tried by the fire he was accused of setting, such as "INCENDIARY TRIED IN A LURID LIGHT" and "TRIED BY A FIRE HE WAS SAID TO HAVE KINDLED." Shorter versions kept appearing in small Southern and Midwestern weeklies until mid-January 1904, some placing the hearing at "Dover" or at 2 a.m.

The Black press carried the story only as news. The Savannah Tribune gave it one sentence among its front-page briefs on December 26, the same sentence that ran in white South Carolina weeklies. On January 2 the Richmond Planet reprinted the Norfolk wire word for word under "Held Court at 3 A. M.," without comment.

Accounts differ on the damage: the Evening Star said six horses and mules were badly injured, the Times-Dispatch that some horses were saved, and the wire that "several fine horses" were destroyed. Later wire versions dated the hearing to the morning of December 20 or "Sunday morning," but the Evening Star had already reported it on December 19.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Bynum
bases: A crowd threatened Charles Bynum's life after he was accused of burning a barn, and a justice held an immediate night hearing and sent him to jail to keep him from the crowd; no one was killed, so this is a threatened lynching (A1, A2, A8).

Bynum was committed to jail and not harmed; the crowd that 'threatened his life' over the barn-burning accusation is of unstated size and did not get hold of him (A1, A2, A10). It is a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

Two separate special dispatches from Suffolk (A1, A2), the Norfolk wire (A8, A9) and the Alexandria Gazette's Virginia news column (A10) agree that Bynum was accused of burning Bond's barn and was saved from lynching by a night hearing.

accounts.label: Suffolk special to the Evening Star
accounts.gist: States flatly that Bynum fired Bond's stables and barn after being locked out, and that a justice held a hurry court at 3 a.m. to save him from a clamoring crowd.

accounts.label: Suffolk special to the Times-Dispatch
accounts.gist: Calls the evidence circumstantial but strong, gives the case against Bynum (refused work or rent, locked out, no account of his whereabouts, said to have made threats), and quotes the officers that his life was in danger.

accounts.label: Norfolk wire report
accounts.gist: Justice Morris held court at 3 a.m. by the light of the fire Bynum was accused of starting, to save him from lynching; horses, vehicles, implements and cotton were destroyed and he was held for court.

framing.detail: Local Virginia specials called Bynum 'an alleged firebug' yet stated as fact that he 'fired' the barn, and presented the night hearing as officers saving his neck from 'the vengeance of the clamoring crowd' (A1, A2).
Papers from New York to Nebraska ran the Norfolk wire under curiosity headlines such as 'INCENDIARY TRIED IN A LURID LIGHT' and 'TRIED BY A FIRE HE WAS SAID TO HAVE KINDLED'.
The Savannah Tribune ran a one-sentence brief and the Richmond Planet reprinted the wire under 'Held Court at 3 A. M.', both without comment.

versions.value: About 3 a.m. Saturday, Dec. 19 ('this morning' in a Dec. 19 dispatch; fire 'last night' and on 'Friday night')

conflicts.note: The Evening Star printed the hearing on Dec. 19, so it cannot have taken place on Dec. 20; the later wire's 'this morning' and 'Sunday' appear to come from re-dating the item. A Maryland weekly put the fire on 'last Saturday' (A18).
